overview.intro: Trigonometry at this level stops being about triangles and becomes the algebra of circular motion. The chapter opens by measuring angles the way calculus needs them — in radians — and then builds the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 that anchors everything else. Compound-angle formulae let an unknown angle be split into two known ones, multiple-angle formulae run that idea in reverse, and the chapter closes by solving equations whose solutions repeat forever. Exact values such as sin 15° and the general solution θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ α are the two products an examination expects to see in working.

facts.label: Radian measure
facts.value: 180° = π rad, so 1 rad = 180/π degrees and 1° = π/180 radians.

facts.label: Arc and sector
facts.value: s = rθ and area of sector = ½r²θ, with θ measured in radians.

facts.label: Fundamental identity
facts.value: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every θ; dividing by cos²θ gives 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Identities and compound-angle proofs carry long-answer marks; equations are steady short questions.

learningOutcomes: Convert between degrees and radians and compute arc length and sector area.
Verify and use the fundamental and derived trigonometric identities.
Apply the compound-angle formulae for sine, cosine and tangent to find exact values.
Use multiple-angle formulae to expand sin 2θ, cos 2θ and tan 2θ and to evaluate exact angles.
Solve trigonometric equations and state their complete general solutions.

learn.title: Radian measure, standard values and the fundamental identities

blocks.text: A radian is the angle that subtends an arc equal in length to the radius, so the whole circle holds 2π radians — the relation 180° = π rad is therefore a definition rather than a formula to memorise. Radians make the arc length s = rθ and the sector area ½r²θ true without a conversion factor, which is precisely why calculus insists on them. The right-then ratios follow the same circle: on the unit circle the coordinates of an angle θ are (cos θ, sin θ), which makes sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 the equation of the circle itself. Dividing that identity by cos²θ and by sin²θ produces the two companions 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ, and the signs of all six ratios fall out of the quadrant the terminal side lies in.

items: Degree to radian: multiply by π/180; radian to degree: multiply by 180/π.
Arc length s = rθ and sector area = ½r²θ, both requiring θ in radians.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ follow from one another.
ASTC rule: sine is positive in quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, tangent in I and III.
Standard values: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° for all six ratios should be recalled without hesitation.

items.note: Apply whichever conversion factor cancels the unit you are leaving.

items.text: A circle of radius 6 cm cut by 2π/3 rad: arc = 6 × 2π/3 = 4π cm, sector area = ½ × 36 × 2π/3 = 12π cm²
items.note: Substitute into s = rθ and ½r²θ with θ kept in radians.

blocks.text: The compound-angle formulae express the ratio of a sum or difference of two angles in terms of the ratios of each angle alone, and they are the working engine of the whole chapter. Sine takes the form sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B, cosine runs with opposite signs as cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B, and tangent is the quotient of the two. Their power lies in combining a known angle with another known angle: 75° is 45° + 30°, 15° is 45° − 30°, and neither appears in the standard table. Setting B = A recovers the double-angle results immediately, so the multiple-angle formulae are consequences rather than separate facts to learn. Sign errors are the common failure — cosine alone changes sign across the bracket.

items: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B.
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B — note the opposite signs.
tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) / (1 ∓ tan A tan B).
Substituting B = A gives the double-angle formulae in one line.
Use the identity with the angle split that both parts are standard: 75° = 45° + 30°, not 60° + 15°.

items.note: Apply sine addition, then put both terms over the common denominator 4.
Cosine subtraction flips the sign between the products.
Rationalise the numerator and denominator by multiplying through by √3.

items.text: sin 75° can also be written cos 15°, since the two are co-functions of the same angle
items.note: Complementary-angle identities connect the two families.

blocks.text: Replacing B by A in the compound formulae produces the double-angle family: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ, cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ, which through the fundamental identity rewrites itself as 2 cos²θ − 1 or 1 − 2 sin²θ, and tan 2θ = 2 tan θ / (1 − tan²θ). The three cosine forms are the most useful line in the chapter, because the right one depends on what is known: the sin² form when a sine is given, the cos² form when a cosine is given. Triple angles follow by writing sin 3θ = sin(2θ + θ), giving sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ and its cosine twin. The formulae also run forwards to exact values: taking cos 2θ = 1 − 2 sin²θ with θ = 18°, and noting 2θ = 36° = 90° − 54°, yields the standard results sin 18° = (√5 − 1)/4 and cos 36° = (√5 + 1)/4.

items: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ; cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 2 cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2 sin²θ.
tan 2θ = 2 tan θ / (1 − tan²θ), valid whenever tan θ and tan 2θ exist.
sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ and cos 3θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ.
The three forms of cos 2θ let you choose the one that eliminates the ratio you do not know.
Half-angle readings: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2 and cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.

items.text: Given sin θ = 3/5 with θ acute, cos 2θ = 1 − 2(9/25) = 7/25
items.note: Choose the sin² form so the unknown cosine never appears.
Substitute into the triple-angle identity as a self-check of the formula.

blocks.text: A trigonometric equation has infinitely many solutions whenever it has one, because the ratios repeat every full turn. The particular solutions inside 0 ≤ θ < 2π are the principal set; the general solution adds the periodicity back and is the answer an examination asks for. Three standard results cover almost every case: sin θ = sin α gives θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ α, cos θ = cos α gives θ = 2nπ ± α, and tan θ = tan α gives θ = nπ + α, with n standing for any integer. Equations that are quadratic in one ratio — 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 — factorise first and then apply these results to each root, discarding any value of the ratio that lies outside [−1, 1]. Identities reduce the rest: an equation mixing sin² and cos² becomes an equation in a single ratio before it is solved at all.

items: Principal solutions lie in 0 ≤ θ < 2π; the general solution counts every coterminal angle.
sin θ = sin α ⇒ θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ α; cos θ = cos α ⇒ θ = 2nπ ± α; tan θ = tan α ⇒ θ = nπ + α.
If the equation is quadratic in sin θ or cos θ, factorise and solve each root separately.
Reject any root with |sin θ| > 1 or |cos θ| > 1 — the ratio cannot exceed one.
Replace sin²θ by 1 − cos²θ (or the reverse) to reduce the equation to a single ratio first.

items.text: sin θ = 1/2 with 0 ≤ θ < 2π: θ = π/6 or 5π/6
items.note: Both angles have sine 1/2 — the first quadrant reference angle and its supplement.

items.text: 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 factors as (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0
items.note: sin θ = 1/2 gives π/6 and 5π/6; sin θ = 1 gives π/2 — three solutions in [0, 2π).

keyPoints: 180° = π rad, so every conversion is one multiplication by π/180 or 180/π.
Arc length s = rθ and sector area ½r²θ both require the angle in radians.
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 generates 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.
sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cosine alone reverses the sign pattern.
cos 2θ has three forms — cos² − sin², 2cos² − 1, 1 − 2sin² — chosen to match what is known.
sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ and cos 3θ = 4 cos³θ − 3 cos θ follow by expanding the sum.
General solutions: sin θ = sin α gives θ = nπ + (−1)ⁿ α; cos gives 2nπ ± α; tan gives nπ + α.
Quadratic equations in sin θ or cos θ factorise first, then each root is solved separately.
Reject ratio roots with magnitude above 1 before solving — they are extraneous.
Exact values such as sin 15° = (√6 − √2)/4 come from compound angles, not from tables.
examFocus: Show the identity transformation one line at a time; each valid manipulation carries its own method mark even when the final line is missed.
Write the compound-angle formula before substituting values — markers award the recalled formula separately.
In equation questions, state the quadrant reasoning for each principal solution before giving the general form with n.
When using a double-angle form, say why you chose it (what is known, what must vanish); the choice itself is assessed.

vocabulary.meaning: Angle subtending an arc equal to the radius; π rad = 180°.

Sum or difference of two angles, as A + B.
Twice a given angle, 2θ, expanded through the compound formulae.
Solution lying in one principal period, usually 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
Expression with integer n giving every solution of a trigonometric equation.
One of the four regions the axes divide the plane into.
Acute angle sharing the magnitude of a given ratio, used to place a solution.
Property of repeating ratios every 2π, or π for tangent.
Algebraic root rejected because it violates |sin θ| ≤ 1 or the domain.

questions.prompt: The radian measure of an angle of 180° is:
questions.explanation: By definition 180° subtends half the circle, and a full circle is 2π radians, so 180° = π rad.

questions.prompt: The exact value of sin 75° is:
Which of the following is a correct form of cos 2θ?
questions.explanation: cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ rewrites as 2 cos²θ − 1 or 1 − 2 sin²θ through sin²θ = 1 − cos²θ; only 1 − 2 sin²θ is listed correctly.

questions.prompt: The general solution of sin θ = 0 is:
questions.explanation: sin θ vanishes at every multiple of π — both 0 and π give zero — so θ = nπ for any integer n.

questions.prompt: The radian measure of an angle of 30° is ______ .
questions.explanation: Multiplying 30° by π/180 reduces to π/6 radians, one sixth of a half-turn.

questions.prompt: The arc cut off by an angle θ in a circle of radius r has length ______ .
questions.explanation: Arc length is radius times angle in radians, s = rθ, which is the very definition of the radian.

questions.prompt: State the compound-angle formulae for sin(A + B) and cos(A + B).
questions.answer: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B, while cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B. The sine expansion keeps the same sign between its terms; the cosine expansion reverses it.
questions.explanation: The sign contrast between the two expansions is the detail examinations test, since it is the usual source of error.

questions.prompt: Find the exact value of sin 15° using a compound-angle formula.
questions.explanation: Split 15° into two standard angles, apply the sine difference formula and combine the terms over the denominator 4.

questions.answer: Using the double-angle identities, sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ and 1 + cos 2θ = 1 + (2 cos²θ − 1) = 2 cos²θ. The left side becomes 2 sin θ cos θ / 2 cos²θ, and cancelling 2 cos θ leaves sin θ / cos θ = tan θ, which is the right side.
questions.explanation: Substitute the double-angle forms first, simplify the denominator to 2 cos²θ, then cancel one common factor of 2 cos θ.

questions.prompt: Solve 2 sin²θ − 3 sin θ + 1 = 0 for 0 ≤ θ < 2π.
questions.answer: Factorising gives (2 sin θ − 1)(sin θ − 1) = 0, so sin θ = 1/2 or sin θ = 1. sin θ = 1/2 yields θ = π/6 and θ = 5π/6, and sin θ = 1 yields θ = π/2. The complete solution set in [0, 2π) is therefore {π/6, π/2, 5π/6}.
questions.explanation: Treat the equation as quadratic in the single ratio sin θ, factorise, then solve each root within the given interval, rejecting nothing since both roots lie in [−1, 1].
